content:
Ice on Lake Mendota. March 6, 2025.

In Antarctica, a cubic kilometer of ice makes up the IceCube Neutrino Observatory — a detector that records interactions of subatomic particles called neutrinos, according to the IceCube website.

IceCube is operated primarily by the Wisconsin IceCube Particle Astrophysics Center, with support from the National Science Foundation and scientists around the world through the IceCube Collaboration, according to the IceCube website. The IceCube Collaboration involves 58 institutions across 14 countries.

IceCube’s mission is to understand neutrinos and where they come from, according to University of Wisconsin physics professor at WIPAC, Justin Vandenbroucke.

“[Neutrinos] are kind of like electrons but they don’t have any mass, or a charge,” Vandenbroucke said. “Because of that, they basically travel through matter.”

It is rare for neutrinos to hit an atom directly, but when they do, the interaction creates a flash of light — that interaction is what the IceCube observatory detects, according to Vandenbroucke.

This is a very new kind of research, as the original detector was completed back in 2011, and at the time, no one had built a neutrino detector of such scale,  Vandenbroucke said.

The neutrino detector is composed of cables attached to very sensitive light detectors, which are lowered into holes drilled into the Antarctic ice, according to the IceCube website.

“It’s very different from a lot of astronomy,” Vandenbroucke said. “In a lot of astronomy you just look up at the sky and see stars glowing. And that’s because stars are very hot. But neutrinos have to be produced by a more energetic process.”

IceCube researchers are looking to find the sources of the neutrino “glows” detected, according to the WIPAC website. Some potential sources include black holes, Vandenbroucke said, and supernovas, gamma-ray bursts and active galaxies, according to the WIPAC website.

During the 2025-2026 austral summer, the IceCube Upgrade was completed, allowing lower energy neutrinos to be detected by installing new detectors at a higher density. In addition, NSF recently renewed its collaborative agreement with WIPAC to support the operation and maintenance of IceCube for the next five years, Vandenbroucke said. There is still significant work to be done in getting the upgrade up and running, but there are exciting new possibilities to come with it — for example, a nova in our galaxy could explode soon, providing an exciting opportunity for IceCube researchers, according to Vandenbroucke.

“It’s possible that with the IceCube Upgrade you could detect signals from that nova,” Vandenbroucke said.

UW students who are interested in getting involved in research with IceCube should reach out to one of the WIPAC faculty members on campus, or send an email to WIPAC directly at [email protected],Vandenbroucke said.WIPAC is also involved in other research aside from IceCube that interested students may want to explore, Vandenbroucke said.
